name: SQLInjectionSpec
source_title: Requested canonical CrySL source, SQLInjection.crysl — unavailable (HTTP 404)
protocol: Unverified as a CrySL protocol: ContentProvider.delete(uri, selection, selectionArgs) -> SQLiteDatabase.delete(table, whereClause, whereArgs), with a finding when externally controllable SQL-predicate text reaches whereClause rather than being confined to bound argument values.
important_note: The requested canonical SQLInjection.crysl URL was consulted but returned HTTP 404, and the consulted CROSSINGTUD JavaCryptographicArchitecture source-directory listing does not list SQLInjection.crysl. Consequently, com.owncloud.android.providers.SQLInjection is an unverified, finding-package-qualified identity included only to meet the required XSpec naming convention; it is not evidence that this class exists in ownCloud or that it is the detector's actual target. This context describes the representative source/data-flow finding, not a verified CrySL protocol or proof of exploitability.

events.name: content_provider_delete_entry

events.condition: Observing either substring identifies a ContentProvider deletion-entry shape only. The predicate requires additional evidence that caller-controllable selection/where text reaches a SQL predicate sink.

events.name: sqlite_delete_sink
events.condition: Observing a SQLiteDatabase deletion call identifies a potential sink only. The predicate requires evidence that its whereClause contains attacker-controlled SQL syntax or dynamically assembled predicate text without independently verified validation.

events.name: selection_argument_binding
events.condition: Observing an argument array or placeholder is not itself proof of parameterization. Binding is supported only when variable values occupy placeholders in a separately controlled WHERE-clause structure and are supplied through the corresponding argument array.

events.name: dynamic_predicate_composition
events.condition: Observing these substrings is evidence of direct forwarding or composition of predicate text. A finding additionally requires attacker-controlled or otherwise untrusted flow into where; a literal or proven-safe predicate is not equivalent to injection.

semantic_scope: The representative finding concerns Android ContentProvider deletion code in com.owncloud.android.providers.FileContentProvider and transfer of its where/selection predicate to android.database.sqlite.SQLiteDatabase.delete. Android documents ContentProvider.delete(Uri, String, String[]) as a deletion handler and SQLiteDatabase.delete(String, String, String[]) as accepting an optional WHERE clause plus values bound for question-mark placeholders.

detector_semantics.claim: The detector reports a potential SQL-injection condition when a ContentProvider delete selection/where predicate is concatenated into, or forwarded directly as, a SQLite deletion predicate without evidence that attacker-controlled SQL syntax has been neutralized.
predicates: A ContentProvider-style delete entry point supplies a String selection/where parameter.
That value flows to SQLiteDatabase.delete's whereClause parameter, directly or through string composition.
The analysis lacks evidence that dynamic values are restricted to SQLite placeholder bindings or otherwise safely validated for the predicate grammar.
For the reported issue shape, security impact additionally depends on an attacker being able to invoke the provider path.
limitations: No SQLInjection.crysl source was available to establish the detector's exact event vocabulary, control-flow sensitivity, taint sources, sanitizers, path conditions, or whether the message is generated by CrySL.
The representative message does not establish the exact source-to-sink path, selected URI-matcher branch, concrete table, or deployed manifest configuration.
Static observation does not establish that SQLite executed attacker-controlled SQL or that an attack succeeded.

documented_behavior: Android documents ContentProvider.delete(Uri, String, String[]) as the provider operation for deleting rows.

Android documents SQLiteDatabase.delete(String table, String whereClause, String[] whereArgs) as a row-deletion convenience method: whereClause is an optional WHERE clause, null deletes all rows, and question marks in that clause are replaced with String values bound from whereArgs.
preconditions: SQLiteDatabase.delete requires a non-null table name.

For documented SQLite binding, the WHERE clause contains question-mark placeholders and corresponding dynamic values are supplied in whereArgs; whereArgs may be null when whereClause is null or has no placeholders.
A ContentProvider implementation is responsible for handling delete requests and applying the selection clause to its deletion operation.

detector_examples.message: expecting ContentProvider SQL predicates to be parameterized or sanitized, but delete concatenates the attacker-controlled where clause into SQLite delete predicates and also forwards it directly for several provider tables.
